questions.question: What is the key difference between an `interface` and a `type` alias in TypeScript?

options.text: They are completely identical with no differences
Interfaces are extendable/merged via declaration merging; type aliases cannot be reopened
type aliases can only hold primitives
Interfaces compile to JavaScript; type aliases do not

questions.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging and 'extends'; type aliases are closed and support unions/intersections better.

questions.question: Which is a valid way to make a property optional in an interface?

options.text: name?: string;
optional name: string;
name string?;
name!: string;

questions.explanation: The ? postfix marks an optional property.

questions.question: Can an interface describe a function signature?

options.text: No, only type aliases can
Yes — interface Fn { (a: number): string }
Only with 'class'
Only for arrow functions

questions.explanation: Interfaces can declare call signatures, index signatures, and construct signatures.

questions.question: Declaration merging means...

options.text: Two interface declarations with the same name are combined
Interfaces are minified at build time
They become classes
They are deleted from the output

questions.explanation: Multiple interface declarations with the same name merge — useful for ambient/global augmentation.

questions.question: An interface with only an index signature `interface Dict { [k: string]: number }` means...?

options.text: Exactly one property allowed
Any string key maps to a number value
Keys must be numbers
It is invalid syntax

questions.explanation: Index signatures describe the type of all properties accessed by that key type.

questions.question: Which is preferred for describing React/Angular component props in most codebases?

options.text: A class
An interface (e.g. Props) or type alias — both common
A namespace only
A function

questions.explanation: Both interface and type alias work for props; convention varies by team.
